title: Snellen screening toy
text:
What it is
A webcam eye test you can run on your own computer. It shows a chart of classic Snellen letters, “Tumbling E” shapes or Landolt C rings, sizes them to how far you are from the screen, and tests each eye in turn.
The demo runs entirely in the browser: the camera stays on your device and no video is uploaded. It needs a webcam and a bank card (or any card the same size), which is used as a ruler to measure the screen and calibrate the camera.

title: Snellen screening toy
text:
What I built
Rapid deployable eye testing is still stuck in the 20th Century, with most online Snellen tests requiring a tape measure, a television sized screen, rock-steady seating, and a second pair of hands.
This project aimed to use a computer vision solution so lightweight that it could run in-browser, with the added benefit of keeping all patient data on their own device, so no strict patient confidentiality to worry about.

title: Snellen screening toy
text:
How it works

The same Python package runs on the desktop and in the browser. In the browser, Pyodide runs it with numpy and OpenCV.
MediaPipe’s Face Landmarker tracks the face; a bank card, held to the screen and then to the forehead, gives the scale for the screen and the camera.
Chart sizes come from the same geometry code in all versions, in device pixels, and font resizes dynamically as the patients’ head changes distance from the screen.

title: Pupil dilation as a treatment marker
text: Case study

title: Pupil dilation as a treatment marker
text:
The question
Atropine eye drops are used to slow myopia in children: the eye grows too long, and the drops slow that growth. They also dilate the pupil, as a side effect you can see without any special equipment.
So: can atropine-induced pupil dilation flag whether myopia treatment is working? If the children whose pupils dilate more are also the ones whose eyes grow more slowly, a pupil measurement could become a cheap, visible early sign of treatment response.
The data was a clinic’s export from an IOLMaster, a machine that measures the eye’s length (axial length) and pupil size at each visit. This page is about the reasoning more than the model. Most of the work was deciding what question the data could actually answer, and making sure the answer couldn’t be quietly steered.

title: Pupil dilation as a treatment marker
Pupil dilation as a treatment marker
text:
Rigour
The pipeline runs in fixed phases, and each one feeds the next:





flowchart TB
  subgraph data ["Data (shared)"]
    direction LR
    A["IOLMaster export"] --> B["Clean<br/>test records, age rule,<br/>ID checks, de-identify"]
    B --> C["Quality flags<br/>flag, don't delete"]
    C --> D["Features<br/>growth rates,<br/>pupil split"]
  end
  subgraph analysis ["Analysis (per question)"]
    direction LR
    E["Locked plan"] --> F["Stepwise<br/>mixed models"]
    F --> G["Diagnostics"]
    G --> H["Sensitivity<br/>analyses"]
  end
  subgraph reports ["Reports"]
    direction LR
    I["Technical report"] ~~~ J["Plain-language<br/>report"]
  end
  data --> analysis --> reports







The plan was locked before any model was fitted. The question, outcome, exposure, adjustments, model and every sensitivity analysis were written down, dated and committed first. Any later change is logged with what changed and why, and anything decided after seeing results is labelled exploratory. Try ten analyses and report the one that “worked”, and the p-value means nothing.
Models were built up in steps: time alone, then age, starting eye length and sex, then the pupil terms. Watching coefficients move between steps shows what is explaining what.
STEPS = {
    "1_time": "AL_rate ~ years",
    "2_background": f"AL_rate ~ years + {BACKGROUND}",
    "3_primary": f"AL_rate ~ years + {BACKGROUND} + {PUPIL}",
}
Diagnostics paid for themselves. Residual and leave-one-patient-out checks caught two things: one optimiser reporting convergence at a clearly worse solution (so each model is now fitted with two optimisers and the better fit kept, with both reported), and one “patient” who turned out to be a staff test scan. Both fixes went into the plan’s change log.
Sensitivity analyses, all reported: around a dozen pre-listed variations, including pupil measured at the start of each interval, a population-average GEE model, one eye per patient, different interval rules, dropping flagged scans, and a cluster bootstrap that resamples patients, not rows:
def bootstrap_sample(fu, rng):
    rows = fu.groupby("Pat_ID").indices
    draws = rng.choice(list(rows), len(rows), replace=True)
    # Each copy of a patient becomes its own cluster
    parts = [fu.iloc[rows[p]].assign(Pat_ID=f"{p}#{k}")
             for k, p in enumerate(draws)]
    return pd.concat(parts)
Reported to the STROBE checklist, the standard for observational studies.
Test-driven throughout: about 120 tests cover cleaning, quality checks, features, models, sensitivity analyses and the report build, each written before the code it tests.

title: Pupil dilation as a treatment marker
Pupil dilation as a treatment marker
text:
Two audiences
The analysis produced two reports from the same results. The full technical report has the models, diagnostics, every sensitivity analysis and the STROBE checklist. A separate plain-language report, three pages at most, is for the clinicians: what was asked, what was found, what it does and doesn’t mean for their patients, and no statistical jargon. Both come out of one build command, so they can’t drift apart.

title: About Me
text:
I’m a data scientist born in London and based in Tokyo, always on the lookout for easy AI wins that most people overlook.
With the invention of the Transformer and its heralding in of the new AI Summer, everyone is looking at how LLMs and other frontier models can solve new and interesting problems, but often that outlook leaves behind problems that have been waiting for solutions for years, decades, or even longer; closing these gaps is the name of my game.

title: Receipt OCR
text:
What it is
Petty-cash receipts for a group of restaurants. Staff photograph receipts, Claude reads the shop, date and total, staff check and tag each one, and a manager emails the month’s ledger as an xlsx file to the head of department.
It runs locally as a small web app for now; AWS comes next.

title: Receipt OCR
text:
What I built
Many small businesses in Japan still operate their monthly budgeting using data manually entered by fatigued shop employees who often aren’t trained in spreadsheet formats and standards, leading to the digital equivalent of a hoarder’s cluttered file system.
This project aimed to address these pain points in the simplest manner possible to reduce error at the entry stage by employees, and to reduce the headache for managers who would often spend hours untangling a spreadsheet that has had its formatting and save encoding ruined by inconsistent software across multiple computers.

title: Receipt OCR
text:
How it works

A model (Claude Haiku or Sonnet) extracts the shop, date and total from each photo, and the result is validated before staff see it.
An evaluation command scores the extractors against hand-labelled sample photos.
